input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-261: Analysis of Algorithms. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course provides an introduction to the design and analysis of algorithms. It covers a variety of classical algorithms and data structures and their complexity and will equip students with the intellectual tools to design, analyze, implement, and evaluate their own algorithms. Prerequisites:(CSCI-243 and (CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)) or (SWEN-262 and MATH-241) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

Source excerpts:

[mit-algorithms]
Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.

[opendsa]
OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.

[rit-csci-261]
This course provides an introduction to the design and analysis of algorithms. It covers a variety of classical algorithms and data structures and their complexity and will equip students with the intellectual tools to design, analyze, implement, and evaluate their own algorithms. Prerequisites:(CSCI-243 and (CSCI-262 or CSCI-263)) or (SWEN-262 and MATH-241) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: A disciplined algorithmic solution requires stating precise inputs and outputs, constructing a correctness argument, and then analyzing resource bounds.
beats.example: Sorting an array: Input is an unordered list of numbers; Output is the same list in non-decreasing order; Correctness is proved by loop invariants; Complexity is O(n log n) via divide-and-conquer.
beats.title: The Disciplined Solution Framework
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart with three boxes labeled 'Define I/O', 'Prove Correctness', and 'Analyze Resources' connected by arrows.

beats.claim: Asymptotic notation describes how an algorithm's resource use grows as input size increases, abstracting away constant factors.
beats.example: If an algorithm performs 5n + 3 operations, its asymptotic growth is Θ(n), meaning it scales linearly with input size.
beats.title: Asymptotic Notation and Growth
beats.visualDirection: Plot a line graph with 'Input Size (n)' on the x-axis and 'Operations' on the y-axis, showing a straight line rising from (1,8) to (10,53).

beats.claim: A loop invariant is a condition that holds before the loop starts, remains true after each iteration, and implies the desired postcondition upon termination.
beats.example: In bubble sort, the invariant 'the first i elements are sorted' holds before the loop (i=0), is maintained by swapping adjacent out-of-order elements, and guarantees the whole array is sorted when i=n.
beats.title: Loop Invariants for Correctness
beats.visualDirection: Draw a loop diagram with an oval labeled 'i from 0 to n-1' and a rectangle inside showing 'swap if a[j] > a[j+1]', with a side note: 'Invariant: first i elements sorted'.

beats.claim: Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem into smaller subproblems, solve each recursively, and combine the results to form the final answer.
beats.example: Merge sort divides an array into two halves, recursively sorts each half, then merges the two sorted halves in linear time.
beats.title: Divide-and-Conquer Strategy
beats.visualDirection: Show a binary tree where the root is 'Array', left child is 'Sort Left Half', right child is 'Sort Right Half', and a bottom node labeled 'Merge'.

beats.claim: Recurrences mathematically describe the cost of recursive algorithms by relating the cost of size n to smaller inputs.
beats.example: The recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n for merge sort solves to T(n) = Θ(n log n) via the Master Theorem.
beats.title: Recurrences and Their Solutions
beats.visualDirection: Display the equation T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n in a centered box, with a small arrow pointing to 'Solution: Θ(n log n)'.

beats.claim: Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based access; stacks enforce last-in-first-out (LIFO) behavior; queues enforce first-in-first-out (FIFO) behavior.
beats.example: A stack of plates: the last plate placed is the first one removed; a queue of customers: the first person in line is served first.
beats.title: Core Data Structures: Lists, Stacks, Queues
beats.visualDirection: Draw three side-by-side diagrams: a horizontal line with numbered dots (list), a vertical stack of circles (stack), and a horizontal line with arrows pointing right (queue).

beats.claim: Trees model hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals such as pre-order, in-order, and post-order.
beats.example: A binary search tree stores keys so that left children are smaller and right children are larger, enabling O(log n) search on balanced trees.
beats.title: Trees and Hierarchical Representation
beats.visualDirection: Render a small binary tree with root '5', left child '2', right child '8', and their respective children, labeling edges with '<' and '>'.

beats.claim: Hash tables map keys to array locations using a hash function; when multiple keys map to the same slot, a collision strategy (e.g., chaining or open addressing) resolves the clash.
beats.example: With hash function h(k) = k mod 7, keys 10 and 17 both map to index 3; chaining stores both in a linked list at that index.
beats.title: Hash Tables and Collision Strategies
beats.visualDirection: Show an array of 7 buckets; bucket 3 contains two circles labeled '10' and '17' connected by a small line indicating a linked list.

beats.claim: Graphs consist of vertices and edges; adjacency lists or matrices represent them, enabling algorithms for reachability, ordering, and shortest paths.
beats.example: In a directed graph, a depth-first search (DFS) explores all reachable vertices from a start node, useful for topological ordering.
beats.title: Graph Representations and Traversal
beats.visualDirection: Draw a simple directed graph with three nodes (A→B, B→C, A→C) and label it 'Adjacency List: A:[B,C], B:[C], C:[]'.

beats.claim: Before finalizing any algorithm, verify: (1) inputs and outputs are precisely defined, (2) a correctness proof exists (invariant or induction), (3) asymptotic bounds are derived, (
beats.example: For Dijkstra's shortest path: define input as weighted graph and output as distance array; prove correctness via loop invariant that visited nodes have optimal distances; analyze time as O((V+E) log V).
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Present a checklist graphic with four tick boxes labeled 'Define I/O', 'Prove Correctness', 'Analyze Time', 'Analyze Space'.

learningObjectives: Students will articulate the disciplined solution framework: define inputs/outputs, prove correctness via loop invariants or divide-and-conquer logic,
Students will distinguish between linear, stack, queue, tree, hash table, and graph representations, explaining how each supports specific operations.
